rationale: The book's core identification — 'to know' as a covenant bond (of the intimate, marital kind) whose reality is proven by obedience, with the unknown person being a covenant 'stranger' — is the reading that best fits the four printed texts taken together. 1 John 2:3-4 states the proof-by-obedience criterion in so many words ('hereby we do know that we know him, if we keep his commandments'); Hosea 4:6 equates the lost 'knowledge' with the forgotten law, not lost information; Matthew 7:23 disqualifies the never-known precisely as workers of anomia (lawlessness), which the book explains directly while a bare 'personal communion' reading must import the obedience link from elsewhere; Genesis 4:1 grounds the marital-union sense the entry invokes, corroborated in the chapter by Hosea 2:20 ('I will betroth thee unto me... and thou shalt know the LORD') and Jeremiah 22:16 ('was not this to know me?'). The strongest specific counter — the mainstream relational-experiential/communion reading, with God's knowing as covenantal election — identifies the same covenantal-relational referent; it disputes only whether obedience is constitutive/probative of the knowing or merely its downstream fruit, which is a mechanism dispute, not a rival core identification. No supplied text is better explained by the counter than by the book; several (Hos 4:6, Matt 7:23, 1 John 2:4, Jer 22:16) are explained more economically by the book because they tie knowing or its absence directly to law-keeping or law-breaking.
book_core_identification: 'To know' (God, or be known by Him) denotes a covenant relationship — of the intimate, marital kind first instanced in Genesis 4:1 — whose existence is proven by keeping the commandments; to be 'not known' is to be a stranger, one outside the covenant household.
book_secondary_elaborations: The marriage typology extended through Ephesians 5:23-24 (bride subject to her Head, so intimacy and obedience are one thing)
The Shepherd composite (John 10): sheep know the voice and follow it; the stranger's voice is teaching from outside the covenant
The claim that anomia underlies most KJV 'iniquity' and links Matt 7:23 to 1 John 3:4
The broader four-word system (love, knowing, faith, belief as four offices of one act of commandment-keeping)
The parallel lexical treatment of 'hate' as covenantal un-choosing (Leah, Hosea 9:15, Malachi 1:3)
strongest_counter_interpretation: The standard scholarly-devotional reading: yada'/ginōskō denotes intimate, experiential, personal communion with God (John 17:3; Phil 3:8-10), of which obedience is the evidence or fruit rather than the defining substance; and God's 'knowing' of persons (Amos 3:2; Matt 7:23; Gal 4:9) is covenantal election — His sovereign recognition and choice of someone as His own, drawn from ancient Near Eastern treaty idiom.
counter_core_identification: 'To know' = relational, experiential communion between God and a person, with the divine side ('I never knew you') meaning covenantal election/acknowledgment; obedience follows from this knowledge as its evidence but does not constitute it.
material_core_denial: For the counter to contradict the book's core it would have to hold that knowing God is an inner experiential state that can exist as the same referent apart from covenant standing and apart from any evidential tie to obedience. But the counter's own proof-texts (1 John 2:3-4; Jer 22:16; Hos 4:6) forge exactly that tie, so both identifications describe the same covenantal-relational referent; the counter only broadens it and demotes obedience from proof to fruit — a dispute over mechanism, not identity.
counter_case: Amos 3:2 and Matt 7:23 fit an election idiom ('recognize as covenant partner') without needing a marital metaphor at all
John 17:3 and Phil 3:8-10 speak of knowing Christ in experiential-participatory terms (resurrection power, sufferings) that exceed a bare obedience-test
The sexual euphemism (Gen 19:5; Judg 19:22-25) covers violent, non-covenantal acts, suggesting Gen 4:1 is idiom for intercourse, not a theological symbol of covenant marriage
Warnings like James Barr's against uniform word-symbol methods caution that yada'/ginōskō is a broad verb whose sense is set by context, not a fixed symbol
1 Cor 8:1-3 and Gal 4:9 make being known by God prior to human knowing, which fits sovereign election more naturally than a bond proven by the human party's obedience
book_explanatory_advantages: 1 John 2:3-4 states the book's core almost verbatim: commandment-keeping is the stated test of knowing Him, and the claimant without it is a liar
Matt 7:23's own disqualifier is 'ye that work iniquity/lawlessness' — the book explains why lawlessness, specifically, voids the knowing; the election reading leaves that clause incidental
Hosea 4:6 internally glosses the destroyed 'knowledge' as 'the law of thy God' forgotten — knowledge lost is law lost, exactly the book's equation
Jeremiah 22:16 defines knowing God by a king's just deeds ('was not this to know me?'), collapsing knowing into covenantal practice
Hosea 2:20 explicitly joins betrothal and knowing the LORD, vindicating the marital elaboration from within the prophetic corpus rather than from homiletics
The 'stranger' element is carried by John 10:5 (sheep 'know not the voice of strangers'), giving the negative pole ('never knew you' = never of the household) a textual anchor
The book subsumes the counter's best texts (Amos 3:2 cited approvingly; Titus 1:16) rather than leaving them unaddressed
counter_explanatory_advantages: Handles the non-covenantal sexual uses (Gen 19; Judg 19) more comfortably as plain idiom
Accounts for the God-first asymmetry of Gal 4:9 and 1 Cor 8:3 via election without routing through human obedience
Avoids the methodological risk of assigning one uniform symbolic value to a very common verb
Preserves the experiential-participatory texture of Phil 3:10 and John 17:3 that an obedience-test summary can flatten
unresolved_objections: Whether obedience is constitutive of knowing or only its evidence/fruit — 1 John 2:3 says 'hereby we know that we know,' which is epistemic proof and does not strictly settle ontology
The marital typology does not govern all uses of the euphemism (Gen 19; Judg 19 describe non-covenantal, even criminal acts), so 'knew' as intercourse is not everywhere covenant language
The book's uniform-symbol method (one established sense holding across the canon) is vulnerable to the standard lexical-semantics objection that a common verb's sense is context-dependent
The divine-priority texts (Gal 4:9; 1 Cor 8:3) fit an election accent the entry acknowledges (Amos 3:2) but does not fully integrate with the bride/obedience framing
Adjacent lexical claims in the chapter (e.g., 'hate' as un-choosing, anomia frequency claims) were not independently verified and are not needed for the core
